content: 1. Needle and syringe programs (NSPs) have been a critical intervention in preventing the spread of HIV among people who inject drugs (PWID). Staff from four new organizations have been trained to provide services related to drug use and HIV prevention. 2. District AIDS Councils have been established in selected districts to reduce stigma and engage both government and public sectors. This initiative aims to facilitate access to health, social welfare, and HIV-related services for clients of Nai Zindagi. 3. Human resource challenges persist for the program, compounded by ongoing stigma, discrimination, and harassment of people who inject drugs, including from law enforcement. These factors discourage the uptake of public sector services. 4. Nai Zindagi is sharing its experiences and technical expertise with similar programs in Nepal, Indonesia, and Kenya. 5. Médecins du Monde (MdM) in Tanzania provides comprehensive harm reduction services for people who use drugs, with a particular focus on women. These services include needle and syringe programs, referrals to opioid substitution therapy, income-generating activities, and legal services. 6. MdM also builds the capacity of non-governmental and community-based organizations to run harm reduction services, including drop-in centers offering a range of support and services. 7. MdM encourages the establishment of dedicated centers and shelters for women, which also provide additional health and support services for their children. 8. National and district-level harm reduction committees have been created with representation from governmental and non-governmental institutions. These committees are responsible for resource mobilization and other activities. 9. Continuous dialogue with municipal, district, and national authorities, as well as sensitization sessions for police, health providers, and journalists, are key components of the program. 10. Partnerships with all sectors of society are considered essential for scaling up harm reduction services across the country. 11. Since 2011, over 6,000 people who use or inject drugs have received harm reduction services. In 2013, more than 2,000 stakeholders were trained in harm reduction approaches and interventions. 12. The Tanzania Network of People Who Use Drugs and audiovisual training for peer educators support empowerment and advocacy activities. 13. Since 2000, Ukrainian NGOs led by the International HIV/AIDS Alliance have provided harm reduction services, reaching up to 23% of the estimated population of PWID by 2007. 14. Peer-Driven Interventions (PDI) were introduced in Ukraine in 2007, leveraging social networks of PWID through incentive-based chain-referral recruitment and peer education. This approach extended services to underserved groups, including women and adolescents. 15. PDI incorporates research components to collect data for tailoring services to specific sub-populations, such as sex workers and street children. 16. Group-level interventions and couples counseling have facilitated outreach to young stimulant users and sexual partners of PWID. 17. Pharmacies have been involved as secondary outlets for distributing injecting instruments and prevention commodities, increasing program coverage by up to 10% in certain areas. 18. Rapid HIV testing in community settings and a case management approach have reduced the time between HIV diagnosis and treatment enrollment. 19. The Women for Women initiative provides gender-sensitive HIV and harm reduction services for women who inject drugs, female partners of PWID, and female ex-prisoners. This program includes services such as gender-based violence prevention, legal assistance, childcare, hygiene supplies, and job placement. 20. Municipal service providers' involvement in harm reduction services has reduced stigma and discrimination against women who inject drugs. 21. In Vietnam, a pilot project decentralized HIV testing and counseling services to commune health stations, promoting earlier diagnosis and treatment. Innovations included fixed-dose ARV formulations and point-of-care HIV and CD4 testing. 22. Community outreach and trust-building have been critical in facilitating earlier access to HIV services among PWID. 23. In Afghanistan, the Afghan Family Guidance Association (AFGA) provides comprehensive HIV prevention, treatment, and care services for female prisoners, focusing on harm reduction for female drug users. 24. AFGA coordinates with the Ministry of Public Health and prison officials to ensure health services are available to female prisoners and to identify injecting drug users for appropriate harm reduction services. 25. In Albania, the NGO STOP AIDS implemented an incentives program to encourage safer behaviors among young PWID. Incentives included vouchers redeemable for retail goods, which improved attendance and uptake of harm reduction services. 26. Methadone maintenance treatment (MMT) was piloted in Kerobokan Prison, Bali, in 2005. The program has since expanded to 11 other prisons and detention centers, integrating with community health services to ensure continuity of care. 27. In Iran, harm reduction strategies, particularly opioid substitution therapy, have been implemented to address a concentrated HIV epidemic driven by injecting drug use. By 2014, over 4,000 drug treatment centers offered OST, with most managed by private sector physicians. 28. The All-Ukrainian Public Center Volunteer runs a program providing HIV prevention services for adolescents in juvenile detention, focusing on those most at risk for HIV infection. 29. Capacity-building initiatives for providers working with vulnerable adolescents aim to increase understanding and sensitivity to their specific needs, strengthening communication and service delivery.
